Telegrams doted from Lahore thin (Setml,v) inorning state that the Cindahar railway was finisliewito Sibi on Wednesday morning. lt is 133 niiles in length, and occupied 110 days in construction. Five thousand men and 2,000 animals were employed, The Quettah extension will soon I, begun. There teems to he no doubt that anarchy pre- vail. at Herat. Ayub is tilt to prison. Colonel 13oisragon ha* driven acros, the river, mar llakko, 5,000 Molitnunds. The inilitory governahip oCeLot iN abolished. -"-Telegrams from Cabul of Saturday's date state that the "discontented and inniguing Afghans”—i.s., people whodo not desire to lone their independence—are notagreed amongst themselttes. The 7'ones cmrespondent has reason to believe, froni smi mos indications, that "the interference of our Go- vernment the affairs of Afghanistan will be gradually acqui- escedthat, the Afghans having now learnt their own , weakness and our strength, the lesson will not have to be repeated." All is quiet at Candahar, from whence we have a report that the Bengal troops are to he :tent back to India and replaced by Bombay regiments. A [elegem from liun- rtamuk gives a very dnfavoumble view of our military and political position in the ennntry which we have "conveyed" front its rightful possesaors. There inn report among the Afghans that the Russians are coming to drive us out. At present the nlcole line of country between the Khyber and Cabal :nay be described as being in an intenxly expectant, not to say feverish condition, and the opinion begins to grow wry strong that longer tlelay on our part in adopting a definite policy may he productive of grave difficulties and complications. Excitement is showing itself among the Mohmunds near our lines, on the further side of Jellalabed, and the truth is that after all the money and valuable lives devoted to the attainment of our objects in Afghanistan be- tween the capture of All Musjid and the present date, our hold on the country is represented in this quarter by little more than a strip of toed about 100 miles long ending, how- ever, in the capital. Colonel Macgregor, chiei cf the staff, has been sent express towarda the scene of the Mohmund excitement, while Colonel Twee lie has been tehgraplied for by General Roberts to join him at ones at Cabid. Messen- gers from Herat are understood to Imre mrived the other day M this neighbourhood with letters for certain local chiefs. Probably the same kind of thing is going on just now in other parts. Well Mahomed Khan, who has been entrusted with the administration of the city of Cabal, inn Sinter of Royal de- scent—in fact, a son of that great Ameer the late Cost Mahomed (ban. By strict Mahomedan custom be is the rightful possessor of the throne, because he is the eldest available male heir of Bost Mabomed. Ile is a younger brother of Yakoob Khan's father. the claim is therefore excellent from a native point of view. But bin readiness to plane himself in the British camp, while his younger brother Neik Mahonled, the posseNs, of the famous Russian teapot, was lighting against UR at Charasiab, is probably his hest title to our favour. Wall Ma homed has four sore, of whom not one has become conspicuous. Ills nomination is r, garded with much hope as the first decisive step in the re- settlement of Afghmistan, which is the most difficult problem of the moment. A telegram from Calml announces tlmt Mahomed Hassan, ex-Governor of Jellalabad, bas made a raid in the Hamra country, destroying many villages, and killing menoromen, and children.

A atudent belonging to—o-ne-oTtshe gymnasiums has been arrested for having posted up seditious proclamations at the atations of the Kieff-Brest branch of the South-Western Railway. A workman employed on this line has alto been arrested for throwing revolutionary papern front a railway . _

The 'lluggiete Courier stales that in several Kazan Tartar villages the Tartars have again revolted, in consequence of the taxes imposed upon them. The Governor, on being in- formed of the outbreak, proc eded to the spot, accotnpanied by a number of police, a detachment of 500 soldiers, and mime officials. It was not until the Governor ordered the whips to he prepared that the Tartars (01 down on their knees and signed a promise to pay the taxes regularly in future. The troops will remain for some time in the villages, obtaining their provisions from the peasantry. The I Vlvire of nuit publishor the following intelligence from St. Petersburg :—Nihilists have just been discovered among the domestic servants and cahte levlroillwe of the If Palace. It loot yet impossible to specify with any degree of exactitude what these (odd remlutionists proposed to do, for the preliminary inquiry if not yet ended, and everything connected with the affair is kept a profound secret, on account of the effect which it is feared the news of the discovery of another conspiracy might have upon the i,eople. Some of the valets rhanthre of the Vl.'inter Palace who were appointed for attendance on the Czar him- self had raised suspicions by their manner, which betrayed a certain unaccountable preoccupation of mind. It was, moreover, discovered that they were in the habit of leaving Ste rooms allotted to them in awing of the palace at night- fall, and of not returning before fonr or five o'olock in the morning. Count Alexander Vladimirovitch Atllerberg, minister of the Imperial household, having been informed of these circumstances by some of the Czar's faithful domestics, gave ordees that the suspected members of the domestic lio,ehold should be watched, and without dolay proceeded to search their rooms. This led to the discovery of Nihilist manifeetoes, pamphlets, proclamations, nod a kind of diary in which the daily occupations and move- ments of the Czar were carefully registered. llis daily habits, the boor of his walks, every particular of his life, were that known to the Nihilists. The conspirators who have just been discovered in the palace are oleo suspected of being accomplices in the attempt made on the life of the , C”r at Moscow, and it is supposed that it is thanks to them ! having by mistake indicated the second train that the Caw escaped death. The Nihilist proclamations seized in the i rooms of these servants of the Winter Palace are printed with type in every respect similar to that of the Imperial printing establishment of the Senate, and it is thought that the printing characters were stolen (rem that establishment by some of the printers employed in it who are in league with the Nihilist committee. 'The Court, as may be imagined, is lathe greatest consternation. The Czar has ordered a nt searching inquiry into the affair, in order that every detail of this latest conspiracy may be brought talight, bet atthe same time has insisted on the affair being a profound secret. The Russian Gov,rnment, e despatch from Berlin affirms, tee addremed pacific notes to the Cabitpds of Vienna and Berlin, in which it expresses its Viiiiioglloe3 to withdraw the troops stationed on the frontiers, if their presence is deemed likely to disturb Iher.f.tntliy,relations which now prevail.
.NATAL.AND ZULULAVD:'

The Natal Mercury of December 15 says "Chief Dunn has been in.Maritzbutg, and has gone loch again, after con- ferring with the authorities. Ho is understood to have stated that the way hart been opened once again for mission work in his territory, and that most of the missionarien had taken advantage of his permission. Mr. Oftebro, we believe holds out for the recognition of his possessory title from, both Panda and CeMwayo. Trade is likely, from all accounte, to be overdone in Zululand, where the young mem. leaving discovered thnt the way to matrimony is actually clear, are marrying in all directions. It is said, indeed, tlmt no mar- riage dowry or payment is being demanded for daughtere! and girls, but Dde is probably an exaggeration. Ukulobola was never among the Zulus the costly process winch it had become in Natal before the marriage low wart paseul. With them muriage was prevented, not by the exactions of me, , smeary parents, but by the order of the king. l'kulobela,! as practised here, was, paradoxically enough, a product of peace and civilisation. Fathers found that young men could earn money plentifully by working, and they raised the prices of their daughters accordingly. In Zululand, where it was forbidden to the 'armed celibates' to work for wages, the price of a wife, except ill the came of chiefs' daughters. woe almoat nominal. We hear that the mi.. sionaries in other districts have had a warm welcome back, ard the Zulu, wonid no doubt be glad to see white men Nettled among them. Tide, however, having beet] forbidden, our Netal natives are stid lobe crossing the boundary in considerable numbers, tempted by the absence of taxation and the facilities for marriage. Differences are said to be imminent between the %aloe and the SIVaZiA, but the story needs confirmation. It is not likely that the traditional enmity between these races will be all at once eradicated,' especially now that the latter Lave taken no prominent and creditable a part in the conquest of Secocoeni. Their bawds about this exploit will do much to irritate and provoke their Zulu neighbours when they return homeward. Are pond. cal weapon this feeling of hatred between Zulu and Swazi , may prove valuable in the future ; but it will need to be I kept in due restraint for some time to come. All will de- I pond upon the amount of European surveillance eatablished along the north-weetern harder. No one seems to know , what arrangements are contemplated in this respect. 'there I should be not one, but several representatives of the (lover. meet in that direction. Ohnin, from all ^accounts, stands in peculiar need of a Iteeitlent. Owing to the position taken ' up by Oh re chief during the war, and to the fact of hie being Cetewayo'a rival brother, he will be the object of jealousiea and animosities which arty impel hint to pereecate and slay those whom he may r tgaol re his foes Nothing is heard of Mr. Wheelwright, nor is it known even whether he meane to retain Ilk post of Resident." In that capacity he prne,edel to the headquarters of the King of Prussi.t ol FediCres in order to arrange an armistice with Bismarck co that the elections for the Constitaent might take ph,. In this mission he failed. and Dr. Busch, in his recent f.koteltes of the great German statesman, repr,nnts Prir...e Bismarck or laughing St the the.itrieal display of angulsh in which M. Jules Fore fa taid to hive infhignol on the occasion. Indeed, the Prince probe-not to beli,ve thot the pallor of the • Frenchman's face 0 the moment when he ploaded force armistice was too dreadful to be natural, and suggested that 31. Jules Fevre most have had recoorse to the paint brush. Although too theatrical lot ortliuiorr political life, Fence's patriotism was unquestionable, and tees eloquent advocate he was second only to Ciambetta. tIER3IANY. The Liberal Whip has recently obtained retarns from nearly every constituency in the kingdom, and the result is eminently satisfactory to the loaders of the party. 'Obey non feel absolutely :Issued of victoryattlie general election, unless the local agents of the party are grossly misinformed or stupidly incapable. It is, of course, never possible to forecast with certainty the emirs° of constituencies under housshold suffrage. They are tossed abont by every wind of opinion, and an eveni might happen between thin end the geneled election whicli would upset all present calculations. Barring any such contingencjr, the estimate of the Liberal managers is that they trill win twenty-slx hormigh and seven coanty seats in England, ton seats in Scotland, and six seats in Ireland, of which, however, four will ito taken by the Home Rulers. Leaving the Horne kale seats out of ViCAP fm- a minute, the total gain of the Liberals will Lk, forty-live, counting ninety on a division. Thus nol only would the I,.ry majority be extinguished, but the Liberals would com- mand acorn and steady majority. The House of Commons consists at present, speaking roughly, of 350 Conservatives,' 250 lAberall,and 50 Home Rulers. The abstraction of 491 votes, inclutinkt the four Home Home Rulers. minces time Conservatives to about 300, and at the same time mires the! Liberal party to about the same number. The balarlce of power, therefore, rests with He Insli party 1 but it is well known that there is a large section of that party who are ! I.iberals 6rol and Home Rulers after. Al kast one-half of them will give a steady support to the Liberal party; and Lord Hartington and sic friends may therefore take oflice, secure for on least a couple of sessions of a considerable and obedient majority.

div.p: STATE OF TIIE IRON TRADE.

A Times correspondent says :—The present slate of the iron trade is of deep importance. If this revival is to strengthen and be maintained d will be an immense gain to the nation ; if it is merely partially solid and based upon eatesdive speculative buying it is well that we should know it ; and if it is promoting an increase of production which must ultimately lead us again to ruin and depression, the sooner a spirit of moderation takes the place of wild excite- ment the better for all concerned.

As a producer of iron and other metals and minerals, it is not my interest to deny advancing prices. I have as much to gain as most men by the improvement but like most of those who are in one way largely interested in the trade, I had to sutler bitterly for the matins. of 1071-2-3, and if by any means the recurrence of such u calamity could be averted the benefit would be great. The Board of Trade returns for the year 1879 enable us to judge of the extent of the revival of demand for iron, mainly for America. The increased export of all amts, in- cluding steel, tinplates, and old rails, and scrap-iron, reached the respectable extent of 583,000 tons over the year 1878. As, however, the production in previous years had been in CACC43 of rouirements and stock accumulated largely, it ap- pears that 01e increase at export combined with the reduc- tion of production in Cleveland through the Durham strike just balanced supply and demand. The already large stock of pig iron in Scotland increased 60,000 tons, while that of Cleveland has diminished to extent of 54,000 tons. Same stock trod accumulated in Cumberland which has disap- peared. and the result for the yew is, perhaps, an excess of delnand over supply, which, however, would not h., been lb, case but for the strike alluded to. The justification for the great rise in prices, varying from 7010 120 per cent., is, theiefore, to be found, not in aletlog excess of demand over supply, as was experienced in 1871 and 1872, but in the expectation of such exce.ive demand. It is worth LIB° examining whether this expectation is likely to be fulfilled. The most marled result of the advance in prices, so far, is not increase of consumption, but of production; there has, ' '

indeed, been large buying bv merchants as well as by specu- lators, but the increased thnsumption has Lien confine.; chiefly an America. From the increase of furnaces actually in operation and certain to be blown in shortly we get the following figures. as the incrmsed supply in sight for 1880 over 1879 :—Cleveland and North of England, 500.000 tons; Cumberland, 400,000 tons; Staffonlshiro, Wales, Lincoln. sure Derbyshire, Lancashiro, and Northamptonshire, 350,00) ton;; and Scotland. 200.000 tons, showing a total increase of 1,450.000 tons. In addition to this, preparations are being mane to start additional furnaces to the number of 37—there will likely be more—and these may be exptcted to be patio Nast in the coarse of the next three months, end will yield a further 250.000 tons, making an increase of production over 1879 of 1,700,000 tons. As regards the probability of sach na increased supply being taken off, it is. of course, impossible' to speak with certainty. A further considerable increa9e of consumption in America my un- questionably be looked for; but there, too, the increase of production isgoing on at an alarming rate. Mr. Malice, of Middlesborough. whom remarkably well-informwl statistics have just been published, esthnates the probtble production of pig iron in 1880 at 4,000,00) tons, as against 3,200,000 tons in 1879; no that, even if the expected increase of 5.000 miles of railway construction be realised, taking 500,000 tons of iron and steel, it would seem that America is making a pretty good provision for her own wants. From other parts of the world indications are not favour- able. October, Nov,tuber, and December show each a de- crease in exports to all parts excopt America, aggregating 00,000 tons, as compared with 1878. It most not either he forgotten that much of the iron bought lately by America has been to 0 large extent .bonght speculatively, and put into store on its arrival. A repetition of this process has now begun, owing to a great rise in fire price of American pig iron, and no doubt occs glottal bursts of such buying may he looked for in a time of great activity and wealth in America ; but in this state of matters periods of cessation of such purchases must inter- vene, as, for instance, was the case in November. . . . .

! On the whole there is ere d reason to fear tbat pro Motion is being overdone considembly everywhere, and witb a stock of over 1,(XXl,000 tons of pm Won in Scotland nal Cleveland, it would be well that the present increase of manufacture shall he proved to be required before further furnaces are blown in. The heat commentary on the wild confidence and excitement of te-day is a consideration tel the Morin anal do- pression of scarcely four months ago. A comparison of both periods is absolutely ludicrous. We only want the appear- ance on the scene of thou promoter " of iron companies to complete the picture. Ife will come.

div.head: LIVERPOOL POLITICS.
div.p: LIVERPOOL POLITICS.

A political straggle of great importance, md awe to which the attention of the whole country will be directed for the next two or three weeks, hm com- menced in Liverpool. Both political parties have selected their candidate for the seat in Parliament rendered vacant by the death of Mr. Torr, and there can he no doubt that immense efforts will Le made on both aides to securs a victory. On Thursday evening the Liberal " DUO " met in Hope Hall, when Lord Ramsey was in attendance, and made no very favour- able no impression that he was formally adopted eon fitting Liberal representative for the great Betsey town. It is a very important circumstance, and one that augura well, that ou his arrival in Liverpool on Wednesday, and after holding a consultation with the leaders of the Liberal Association, Lord Ramsey left for Knowsley, whero he remained as the honoured guest of the Rail of Derby. It may be at once admitted that the Knowsley influence has always been a factor in Liverpool Parliamentary elections, that must not be left out of the calculation in eatimating the chances of a Liberal success. It is a matter of histoty that at all former electiom in Liverpool the Knowsley influence has been one of the greatest stumbling Mocks that the Liberal party have had to contend against so that the mere withdrawal of that influence would be a great gain. But we are justified in saying that the cones which Lord Derby has re- cently pursued, and the very unreserved manner in which he Las spoken against the t' gunpowder and eery " policy of the present Government, make it imp.ssiblo for him to retrace his steps or to find his way back to the Tory camp. The more than proba- bility is that, like Mr. Gladstone, the breach between him and Toryism will grow wider. As time goes on, he will keep touring, slowly, perhaps, and cautiously, but not the km stesdily and continuously, towards the party of progress and of advanced and enlightened Liberaliem. Born and bred in "the purple" almost from the earliest years of his public life, he has always shown the strongest possible desire to benefit the masses of the people, and to support any popular measure calculated to improve the material condition of the poorer and working classes, whether in the towns or counties. That a man so gifted and so placed, and yet in the very prime of life, must have a great and important I store before him as a Liberal statesman is indeed most probable. But, as far as the Liverpool election is concerned, what is of greater im- portant, than Lord Derby's influence is the well- known fact that as a seceder from the Beaconsfield administration he is a representative man. In Liver- pool, as elsewhere, there moat he many thousands of electors who might have been deacribed five or six years ago as moderate Comervativett, but who certainly will no longer support the new high - handed Tory policy of which Lard Beaconsfield is the originator. The eo • called moderate " men, who in lull began to think that the Liberals were travelling a little too fast, foolishly Imagined that by voting Conservative they would put on the drag fore short time. They are now bewil- dered and disappointed at finding that instead of doing so they have stopped the coach altogether! They hate had a bitter experience; and the lemon which Lord Beaconsfield, with an obedient Tory majority at his back, Las taught will, it is to be hoped, not be thrown away, at :east during the pre- sent generation. The recent municipal elections at Liverpool furnished unexpected evidence of the force of the current of public opinion running against the Government and its policy, both home and foreign. But it will be most unfortunate for them, and the moot discouraging blow they have yet received, if the Parliamentary constituency of Liverpool, as a whole, Mould endorse the very emphatic verdict pro• nounced by the municipal electors in November. Some Tory writers argued that the maniciral elections could be no fair test of the politics of the borough, inasmuch as in all such conteats there are local reasons for electing one man rather than another, irrespective altogether of his political views. But, should the municipal Liberal viapries be followed up by the return of the Liberal candidate at the Parlia- meetary election, the cuudemnation of the Govern• meat policy by the largeat and moat important con- stituency in the Three Kingdoms, outside of London, will be complete.

Thar Liverpool electoral contest will undoubtedly be the most interesting and important trial of strength between the two great political parties into which the country. is divided that can take place previous to, or even during, the general election. This is so partly on account of the peculiar wins at which it occurs, and on account of the fact that in Liverpool there are not so many bye issues to affect the result, as there were at Sheffield, for instance. The strongest and most unhallowed influence against which the Liberals will have to fight is that of the brewers and all those engaged in the drink traffic. But on the banks of the Mersey there are no 1 ichbornites and Riebuckites, that we are aware of, to distract the attention of electora from the plain issue that will be placed be- fore them, as to whether they are the opponents or the supporters of the policy of her Majesty's present Government. Then there are the Home Rulers, a turner°ae body in Liverpool, who are not to be seduced, either there or elsewhere, from their loyalty to the Liberal party. Some time ago it was announced that the leaders of the Irish party in Liverpool intended starting a candidate of their own; but this idea has been abandoned, and they will vote for Lord Ramsay ea 61... The interest in this coming struggle is, as we have intimated, intensified on account of the peculiar time at which it occurs. The result will be known shortly after the opening of Parliament, and before there is any time for attempt, tube made onothe part of the Government to bring back waverers by promises id' amendment in the future. The Liverpool electors will have to say what they think of the per- formances of tho Government during the last five years. Their exploits abroad may be roughly sum- marised' by mentioning the unfulfilled Berlin Treaty, , the unsuccessful occupation of Cyprus, the needless and cruel invasion uf Zululand, the exploded Treaty of Gundamuck, and that puzzle for the Geographical Society—the scientific frontier. While as to their home policy, it is, att Mr. Chamberlain says, host represented by that black, blank panel to be seen in the palace at Venice, and which was placed there in memory of some particular Doge about whom there was nothing good to record. As they stand to-day, the Tory leaders know full well that they have prac- tically no defence for their action during the pest that will have any weight with any of these electors who are of Lord Derby's way of thinking. In the face of this state of things the Premier will not dissolve, be- cause, as Mr. Gladzioce said at Warrington, be" dare not dissolve." Before the dissolution there must be another session of Parliament, and it is broadly stated that in the meantime Ministers purpose &deg some wonderful expl, it'. Those ingenious gentlemen who stipply the provincial daily papers with London goarip tell us that the air it full of rumours of the great things that are robe performed in this the last year of their existence, by a penitent Tory Government. We are to have a Pialiamentary session of repentance and humiliation for past errors, and of promises of future good behaviour. One of these correspondents, writing on Wednesday, says :—" Shrewd, far-seeing kolnicians here are convinced that the Prime Minister

hem great intentions for the coming ewsion. The question of Parlinrorsatary reform in one oi the historic , I not for. ditary duties decory sucoeasive Government. Lord Ber,ensfield is nothing if not historic, and his ambition has always included in its wide-sweeping range the desire to settle the Twerion of Poliamentary reform for another half-century. That the coming , session will be crowded with "importune latainma" ; , quite apart from coenty franchise reform, is nuffi.; dead,- obvious already. First and foremost, the 1 Ballot Act, • Lich expires this year, must be renewed. Then the Chancellor of the Exchequer has given m I undertaking to the House of Commons to provide for the are vacant mats,—• matter which, like the renewal I of the Ballot Act, is not likely to pus: over without exciting the attention befitting its importance. Again, I the question of the extension of polling hours will ' orme up for settlement. Here are three matters each I intimately connected with Parliamentary reform, and all containing the Elements of party debite." The same writer mentions the rumour that there are "two great ,ops"—oae for the County Franchise on • household harts- soother for Ireland to settle the land prestion "in a pennant propriemry direotion." But whether there he a kernel f truth in any of these vaticinations, and that the Beaconsfield Administra- tion intend seriously to attempt to play the refs, at the elrventh hour, of conse-ience-strickeri and iv- pentmt sinners, can have little or no effect on the minds of Liverpool electors at present. They will be called upon to return their representative elom upon the day of the opening of Parliament and the delivery of the Qtreen'a Speech. If the Liverpool verdict heart adverse one for the Goverurnent, it will be so In avy • blow, and so ; rout a dimouragement, as to make it impossible for them to go to the country" with any reasonable hope of success. And , more than that— the cry fee an inarnediate dissolution will boccie° louder and more earnest than ever. The devethment will find that to postpone the issue longer can be of no avail. They will become eon- ' vinced that the day for repentanee and god resolves • to be of service has passed, and that of judgment has come when the country will insist upon rt turning its verdict upon their bygone nets alone.

div.p: THE IRON TRADE.

The rapid inflation of prices in the iron (lade is regarded Iv many cloee observers as one not likely to to or:\ pgrman- eat charagter. Other obsenwra, with as keen perception and long experience, take an opposite view, and cenduct thsir bus Mess accordingly. The :improvement which has taken place in that branch of industry haii undoubtedly pro- moted an activity in other traded that hae not been witnessed for some ycers. Our manufactures and commerce have been almost at their lowest ebb, nod the poverty of COIII. munities hart been correspondingly intensified, so that signs ! of • happier future have been welcemed, ne matter from what source they have sprung. The buoyancy in the iron trade ie undoubtedly due to • large demand from the United States for iron to be uced chiefly in the extension of the railway system in that vast and thrivingeoutinent. America has itself ported through a period of severe depression, but luckily for its people it hes bcen favoured with rich and large crops of agricultural product, whilst in England the chequered weather has in moet places been 1,11110. to the growth and the ingathering of the fruits of the soil. This circumstance has enabled the agriculturists America to find on this aide of the Atlantic a ready market aml good prices for theirprod Lice. and they bare thus become not oce y the priucipsl purveyors of foml for the pceple of this country, but capable of investing capital in such under. takings as have given impetus to the iron teal,' a England. hila we are rejoicing at the revisal of our trade, and in our innocence suspecting that that revival will lce minium COIN it is as well that we ehould he reminded of the ( act that America posaesnes within her own confines undeveloped sources of metallurgical products that must render her, in ceuree of time, indepmdced of the Ohl World. In the New World there are vast &Ids of iron ore that have not yet yielded ensiling for the farnaces, because of the absence of mean, of transit. The intercection of the country with railways, however, will render these tieids of mineral. accessible, and lead to their development. The Ainericens, therefore, as aoso as they can cross their extensive prait•in and enrol Ii Vat,i tracts of territory with good roads and a comprehensive eystem of railwap, will b.- in a position to 11,104 niece extensively than at present our own markets with agricultural !nodose and will set about iodisententhfromohco kmwele of their own soil metals the demand for which has iniparted briskness 00 1110 trcele of this country. Possessing an enor- mous area of virgin aoit, capable of producing food to an immeasurable extent, and etored to an almost unlimited degree with metallurgical products, Amerioo promises ere long to take a prominent position in the front make of the commercial nations of the world ; and it will he wise in the! • commercial men of the Old Country not to depend upon the buoyancy now expgrienced lunar Gun mark-is being con- tinued by reason of the demand. from America for English ' iron.

P. RYLAND:, On THE POLICY OF THE GOWER-, YENT.—A crowded inertio, of the Liberals of Stockport IT. held on Ttiesday evening in the 3lechanics' Institute, to hear an address from Mr. P. Eyl.mds, M.P., on the policy of the Governintnt. 31r. F. Pennington, 31. P., oecupied the chair, and the other member for the borough, Mr. C. H. Hopwood, QC., was pi es.t.—The Chairman spoke at mme length in intraliming Mr. Ryland*, who severely criticised the policy of the Governo,ni, especially in relation to foreign affairs. He affirmed that to find a parallel to the blundering in- capacity cud dangerous policy of Lord Beaconstirld, it wan necessary to go back at least a hundred vears, to the Govern- ment of herd North. Lord Beaconsfield, he inaintained,had prostitutal the British power in supporting despotism and in strangling the rights and liberties of nationalitiee strug- gling for freedom. The issue lobe determined at the next general election was whether the policy which was now being pursued should continue or not. (Hear, hear.) He observol that at a Tory meeting hal in Stockport the other night Mr. Wilbraham Egerbm drew a contrast between Lord Beaconsfiehl and M. Gladstone, in which he attempted to show that Lord Beaconsfield WAS by for the greater patriot, and that his policy conduced more to the honour of this country. He entirely disagreed with the judgment of Mr. Wilbraham Egerton as to the respective merits of the two statesmen, but he fully agreed with him in the statement that the next general election would be decided upon that very question. (Cheers.) No two statesmen could be more completely apart front one another or more completely dif- ferent from one another than Lord Beaconsfield and 3D. Glad- stone. The country would have is choose between them. They would have to choose Ixtween the policy of Lord Beaconsfield, which worn policy of "glory and gunpowder" and of a political bandit, or the poliey of Mr. Gladstone, which was besot upon that great and golden rule in refer senor to nations, " Do unto others as vou would have others do unto you." (Loud cheers.) They had all, no doubt, read in those speeches which Mr. Gladstone had delivere.l In tiebtlard the programme of the Liberal party for the future. He belireed tha they would all be willing to exert Unwisely.e to carry out that programme. (Cheers.) But there Ho,,' duty thev would have to perform before they could enjoy the benefits of Mr. Gladstone's administration ; that duty f1,..y would have to perform by their ve!e and by heir rErrtg., at the Cection, woe simple and blear it was to dri‘e from p.nter 010,100 Minister who had soiled and fouled the name of Great Britain in the councils of Europe, and who had impa.red and injured the prosperity of their countrymen CO home. (Loud and continued cheer. ing.)

Cuesaino Wounttes —Warburton, Rowland, a Chaahlin man, and a member of the Arley family, has been made immortal in the old ballad called a Ledy Bessye," as pub-, Baled in Percy's collection. Sir William Shtnley war balievrd to hang lire when the fate of England lay in the balance on the ere of the battle of Bosworth. Itichant did not fully trust bin, nor did Beery of Richmond; but, if we art to accept the testimony of the old ballad, and adopt it for history—which may often be done with eefety—Stanley bad, in fact, made up his mind to support Richmond, and only pretended ta stand neuter in the cornin,,,, struggle. He is made to lee at Holt watching the wind and enquiring from his followers how it standeth. On being informed that it astandeth now south-west," he exclaimed—. This night yonder Royal prince into England entered," meaning thereby Richmond; and then— lie called that genthman that stood hint by. Ills name was ILtdeo.l ifartmrton. He had idni go to Shrewsbury that algid. Arad bad him let that prince In coma.

Wlmtever doubt may have booherished as to Stanley's mal, there can be none as to the energy and baste with which brave Rowland Warburton fulfilled hie nilsaion ; "for theee Cheshire squires. when they take up a side, enter ups. it with a gallantry and courage,' and it is but reasonable Co auppose that this young gallant did honour to Lis name both at Shrewsbury and at Boswo:th, and madded to the many laurels that had already crowned it in days long pug. The ballad history of England often comes down to or crowned with glory, for it abounds in records of chivalry, and it tells us of deeds done by our brave sires which will for ever live in our most affectionate remembrances. Warburton, Rowland Eyles Egerton, is the eldest eon of the late Rev. Rou land Egerton, of Oulton l'ark, Cheshire. He was born In that coney in the year 1804, and became heir to hie great uncle, Sir Peter Warburton, whore DEMO was assumed by the father in 1813, when he succeeded to the Arley estates. Educated at Eton and Corpus Christi College, Oxford, with ample means at his command, Mr. Warburton, as might be expected, hair spent his life at home as a country gentleman, serving the office of High Sheriff and fulfilling other ordinary duties of a person of distinction; but he claim. notice in these records as the author of ',Hunting songs and miscellaneous verses " of no common order. The work is oue of great excelleece, and of deserved popularity. Upon the quaint text—. For honest hunting never was accounted shine, one never ehall for mee " She author Ste sung a good moral song, encouraging thereby the sport which has done so much to make Englishmen famous horsemen, brave warriors, gallant gentlemen, and if *0 0007 be allowed to say so, loyal and true moo; for puttingpolitice aside, there is nothing so likely to knit men together in defence of their country as the "meet," *here daring and strict obedience to law, go band in hand in puma of the one great object that has brought men together—the fame and glory of the English spostsman.—Osteestry.f.frerfierr. THE IRON son COAL Titan. —Malthus...6a, Wed- nesday.—There is still only a nmderate amount of businese doing in the coal Rodeo( this district, but there is generally a steady tone in the market. There are conaiderable in- quiries for forward delivery, and there is little doubt that large quantities of coal could be sold over the next six or nine months at present rates; but colliery proprietors are not disposed to enter into anything like forward contracts, as there is everywhere a confident feeling that with the sr- in the iron trade and the improvral proepects of the cotton trade, the coal trade mug before long be materially strengthened. Considerable quantities of outside coal have already teen withdrawn from this market in conaequence of the activity in the large iron producing districts, but at present local supplire continue quite eufficient to meet re- quirements, rend there is gill a large margin for increased production, which naturally tends to prevent any material upward movement iu values under existing circumstances. For house-fire classes of fuel there is a moderate inquiry for the tirne of the year, and the lower classes of fuel meet with a fair demand with prices at the pit mouth remaining much the comets HIOW ruling last wool, best coal being quoted at from So. 6d. to Se.; seconds 7s. to 7s. &I.; common round coal. Sr. 6d. to tie. ; burgy, 3s. 9d. lode. 34.; good slack, 3e. to 3. Sri.; ani common, Is. 3d. to lo.fld.per ton. The shipping trade shows a falling off as cumpared with last week. Sellers have not been able to maintain the slightly higher pricee which were being quoted a week ago, as these have brought increased quantitiee of coal into the market, and beg steam coal delivered alongside is not fetching more than Bs. &I. per ton, whilst there is plenty of coal offering at the high level, Liverpool, at from 7s. to Is. 611. per ton. The representatives of the coal trade in the Manchester market met yeaterdav in the large arcade of the Victoria Buildings, where it bas been decided to hold the Mancheiter Coal Exchange in future. Arrangernents base been made for the receipt of private telegrams in the arcade, where it is also proposed to take special offices for the convenience of the trade. There has been rather a quieter market in the iron trade of this district during the past week, and, if anything, there has been a somewhat easier tone in prices, so far as some of the outside brands of pig iron are concerned. This, however, has been chiefly in second-hand 101, makers, as a rule, holding for their full prices, with a strong disinclination to quote for forward delivery, the belief being entertained that priceswill advance still further next month. A strong den and is maintained for forge iron, and for ordinary Finalities local makers are so fully sold for eeveral months to come that they arc averse to quoting at all for the ire,, and considerable stocks of the lower qualities which a Mort time back were scarcely saleable at all, are now being rapidly cleared away. Foundry numbers, however, only meet with a moderate in- quiry, as the quantity going into local consuruption is still much below the average, the principal Lancashire users, eueh or founders, engineers, and machinist& being atill but poorly employed coo rule, whilst they complain that with quotations based upon the present cog of the rary material it is shoret impossible to secure new orders at all. The quota- Brno for Lancashire pig'are without change from laq week, and remain at 70., per ton less 21 for both foundry and forge qualities delivered into the Manchester district. In the liaisherldron trade the tendency of prices is still upwards. Buyers offer freely DI 15s. for bars delivered Into the Manchester district, hot makres who are kept busily employid on orders far export are ruffling .£9 per ton cot upwar&, and some do not care to quote at al/. The following was the report of the Executive Commit.° :—"The Executive Committee beg. , to report its proceedings for the past year. The question of the cost of water by meter, referred to the Committee by the Association, was considered, and the Committee came to the! conclusion that it was not advisable to take any action against the Local Board, as it seemed clear that the water could not be sold for less than its present price without a loss to the ratepayers. The clauses in the London and North- Western Railway Bill, which were objected to by the Aesociation, were withdrawn ; and the Committee ,of the House of Commons refused to grant the increase of maximum Toter of charge which were proposisl by the North Staffordshire Railway Company. The com- mittee has been in communication viith the Loudon and North-Western Itailway Company's officials with reg wit to the blocked condition of the renal and dock entrances, and asked for an interview with tluir representative on the Upper Mersey Commission. This requtst not having been com- plied with, the Committee have forwarded a communication to the Secretary 01 the Commissiontrs, asking him to bring the matter onicially before the Commissionera at their next meeting. The Conunittee has aleo had aortic correspondence with Mr. Kay about the great delays which have occurred in working the (iarston trafli,l. 51r. Kay alleged that the Waders at Widnes hail addod to the didicultiesof the Railway Company by not having sufficient skiing accommodation to take in the waggons and unload them within a reasonable time. To this the Committee urged Bat, even supposing it to be so, it is the duty of the Railway Company to see that !the necessary private aidingr are provided, and that it is no excuse for the delay to toy that the r.sou is that some , traders are short of sidings. The Committee have pressed the point very strongly on Mr. Kay's attention, and urged prompt action, and are itt hopes that the Railway Company will be induced to do what it necesmrv. lf, how- ever, the Railway Company does not move with-in a reason- able time, the Committee suggests that the solicitors be con- suited as retire probability of a successfel trial before the Railway Commissioners, The Loodon and North n -Wester Railway Company have introduced a bill to obtain power. (amongst others) to widen the St. Helens Railway, and, as it , is provided that all widenings are, for all purposes, to be part of the railways widened, there appears no need for the association to oppose. Tim e North Staffordshire Railway Company are again introducing chili to vary the maximum rate of charge clause in their original Act, and the Com- mittee is of opinion that the memorial should he prepared and forwarded to the Bosrd of Trade, drawing attention to the Net, and stating that, in the opinion of the Association, ! a reicia.iscation of goods should be insisted upon before any change is allowed, 'the period for which the President and the /lon. Secs, were appointed having expired, it is necessary for the Association to elect gentlemen to those offices. The balance to the credit of the 18137 account is £.354 11s. 101—T. Surrox nanny, Chairman of Execu- tive Committee."

The following report of Mr. T. &Sandford, H.M.1., on the Warrington.road Seilooi, wan read:—Boys' School r The school continues to be well ordered and taught. The in- struction is sound. and the tone of intelligence is encourag- ing, though capable of still further development, especially in the reading of the highest standards and in arithmetic, as an exercise of thought. A larger number of boys should be able to solve the luestions regniring thought. In the sixth standard composition is poor; in the third standard, spelling, arithmetic, and geography need care; and in the fourth standard arithmetic with grammar must be strengthened. Girls' &hod The order here is quite satis- factory, but there is a feebleness of tone noticeable in the instruction generally, and an absence of sufficient intelli- gence, which, with the extremely defective arithmetic, in- duces me to conclude that the school is not doing as much as it should. No class is really well taught, and in some classes there is a falling short considerably of a respectable standard of efficiency. The penmanship is of poor quality throughout, notation is not known well in the second and third stand:a-Ell spelling is bad in the third and fourth. I shall look for marked improvement next yuar. Infante' , &hoot The infants are very fairly disciplined and fairly ' taught. Considering the advantage under which the mistress works, I think a higher standard should be reached in every ! class net in all subjects, and the children should be more animated and interested in their wmk. The mistress must strive to produce a good average of results, and not be con- tent with aeloontuoght well in one subject and indifferently in another. In adding and subtracting the children enact not allowed to one their fingers. The other business before the Board was not of public interest.

TWO BROTHERS DROWNED.

A melancholy ice accident by which two brothers lost their lives occurred at Weston on Wednesday morning. It seems James Carson (13) and Edward Carson (11) left home for Mr. Craik's schools, I rwell-lane, Runcorn, about nine o'clock in the marning, and on their way they had to passe pit at the corner of Runcorn Common. The pit being frozen over the boys evidently venured upon it for a slide when the ice gave way, and no one being near at the time they were drowned. A girl, named Mary Ga/ nee, going to school, , now a basket on the ire and al,o now the head and hands of , one of the deceased sticking through a hole in the ice. She ! gave an alarm, and some men came up and got the boys out,l but they were quite dead. Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at the Royal Oak, Weston, on Thursday, on the bodies, when the follow- ing evidence was given : John Blair said he lived at the Royal Oak, in Weston, and was a labourer. The bodies the jury had seen were those of lds half-brothers, James Carson and Edward Carson, mns at Thomas Carson, &erased, late of Weston, publican. Jam. was 13 yeam of age and Edward 11 years of age. Both the deceased went M school at Mr. Craik's, in Irwelldlane, Run- corn. He last saw them alive on Wednesday morning, the :Ist inst., at breaktod time. Ile kneve they had to go to school that day, and that they !mil to walk and pass the pit where they Were drowned.

Maly Ann Sefton maul she was the daughter of Joseph Sefton, brickeetter,of Runcorn Common. She teas going to school at Weston on Wednemlay morning, when she met the deceased, whom she knew. James spoke to her. She then passed on, and, on turning round my both the deceased getting on to a pit at the corner of Runcorn Common. The pß:ran (rotor over..

Mary Garner said she was the tlaughter of William Garner, chemical labourer. Runcorn Common. About a quarter to !nine no Wednesday morning she was coming up the lane from the common on her way to school, and as she was passing the pit at the corner of the common, she saw a locket on the or, and the head and hands of one of the deceased , sticking up through to hole in the ice. She told Mary Jane Whitley, who was with her, to go for assistance, and she ! afterwrds overtook the last witness. She did not hear the ice break .or calls for help. .. . „

MUNICIPAL: COILI"DitATI-O—.NS AND LOCAL AU IHORITIES. Sir—Afire many years' experience in Municipal and Pear•taw business, it has often occurred to me that there is a great waste of tune and no increased expenditure of public meaty in the way we manage our local affairs and in the election of oar local representatives. It is not my present intemicit to enter into Si!! statement of grievances, or at- tempt exhaustive arguments to prove ray paints, but simply to give an outline of my ideas, in the hope that what I may say will provoke discussion. an I cause some general attention te the importance of the subject. s In the lira place, I would make the present Poor-Law trui.m. and Parochial Boards of England, Ireland, Scotland, , mid It alcs, the basis of all Local Government, and elect from 1 Townships Local Representatives in proportion to population mad ratable value of property, each Township paying rates according to its expenditure, and so maintain thenld familiar Landmarks. This could easily be done by slight alterations in some Unions, and joining and grouping other smaller ones , tagetiwr. This would divide the whole of the United King. ,i•ln mt., Local Districts, each under a distinct acme, every district In have an elected council, to consist of so many members from every township or group of tovrnellips eleeted Inn ballet hy the ratepayers annually, one-third of their number to rouse every year. 1 would then give the el. otod Council power to elect an additional number of mernher, Lqual to con-third of their number, for pin years, either from themselves or the rates payers, one sixth to retire every year. All extraordinary elections of members to be made to the Council without any appeal to the ratepayers; all rlections to he by ballot; and curnulative voting to be adopted both by the ratepayers and the Council when more thanes person is required lobe elected. • ' " • • .• • • • ^ ••

vroald then elect annually out of tide local Connell the , following representative bodies :ant committees :—First, an 1 assessment committee, to lay ant. collect rates according to the expendlture of each townslup, and to pay precepts for Imperial taxes Second, the board of guard's. for Poor- law purposss. Third, the reload board, to carry oat Os lidueation Act. Fourth, a licensing committee, with full powers to grant all licences fur the sale of intoxicating beverages. Fifth, a sanitary committee, to include, amongst other duties, the control of all cemeteries and burial grounds. Sixth, a highway, bridges, streets, and drainage committee. Seventh, a finance and general purposes committee. This is but an outline of what I mean. Many subsidiary Committees could require appointing for special work in different distric, s ; however, this would bring the control of all expenditure and many subjects of vast importance under the direct supervision of the ratepayers of every township and district, because it should he imperative upon al! Boards and Committees to report their expenditure and proceeding to the tieneral Council for adoption. . . . . .

I also approve of the Central Boards in London having the supervision of all local governing bodies, thinking that Government control, inspection' and auditing of accounts should be goneral throughout the United Kinvdmn. This eyetem of managing our local affairs Would enable as to oho' lob and do away with the trouble, annoyance, and turmoil of to many elections. The expenses connected with the election of ao many public authorities are enormous. We cc,nl,l thus abolish the election of Boards of Guardians, Ore, seers, School Boards, Highway Boards, Town Councils, 80A!..13 of Health, undo large number of local and public officials. The power of Magistrates and of foe Excise to grant any licensee, the power of the County Magistrates to send precepts hr rates, whicil scarcely any pawn can under- stand, besides many old antiquated Act/apt Parliament might far repealed,and our Local Government lowa might be all consolidated into one general Act of Parliament for unlace- admdion in the United Kin,dom. """" " ' • '

-1-;14e; feel almost Certain th-at iliese local municipal districts might be m arranged as to form a more correct basis for Parliamentary election., and thus abolish the present distinction of counties and boroughs, and make oue list of persons entitled to vote sufficient for an purposes; but this tequilas some further corgideration. tam much interested in the subject of this letter, and should be glad to coeoperate with anyone who feels its im- portance, and to join in making further investigation and inquiry iu view of pressing on legislation on the subject.— I am, ate., JOSEPH WHITE. fleath flied, Wakefield.
TIIF WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

.. Sir,—l feel so hurt, sorry, and wounded by the sudden at- tack one member of the Widnes Loot Board by Mr. Harrow. It seems to me that let them think or speak, they cannot give satisfaction to all; there is sure to be some one to worry and tear them to 'deems for simply doing thole daty. A mem- ber of the Board receives instructions in a e ldsper at the top end of the table to go and boy a house and garden. After the sale, thinking he has made a good purchase, he sociably sets Ids friends to have a glass of champagne. Mr. Barrow says it is not lawful to sr end the ratepayers' money either in champagne or md without hie knowledge or letting him know aboutit Who cannot he leave it entirely in the hands of the Cha na , the 221110 as they have handed over the Surveyor's and their plans for the level crossings and sewer- lag belonging to the township ? The well-known ability of the Widnes Local Board in dealing 'WWI level crossinge can- not be called in question i for look how nicely they have worked the footpath that leads from Ann-street East to Moss- bank. What a beautiful road they have made! The ap- proeches to learn something grand! Instead of gicinga nice, gentle slope over the railway, making it twice as long in walking, they put a lot of stone stets. If you have good wind and free from gas, you are up in a twinkling. It is foolish in any one saying the gaslights there are too glaring, and that they would rather walk a mile further round by the Bradley Crossing than come to town that way. I tell them that sort of talk won't do; they cannot appreeiate a good thing. What a splendid eight for a man who has been absent from town about five years to stand oath, top of that bridge and view the old men and women toiling up theme grand steps! He would say to !dined!, let the Widnes Local Board make all their bridges and approaches like this one, and they will earn the lasting gratitude of their fellow- townemen, and their names will be lmnded down to posterity. The fathers of this generation will with rile tell their chil- dren, "This is all done by the Widnes Local Board."—Yours, trc., SATE SOS Wide., January 206, MAO, AN OLD FISHERMAN'S REMINISCENCES OF THE RIVER MERSEY AT WARRINGTON.

...... Sin,—! well remember the time when salmon came up the Mersey at Warrington to feed and spawn in great abundance. They were taken with • draw net, and at time. mid so low as 2d. a pound. It was not unusual to catch them from 501 MBO pounds in weight. Near the bride, and even upon it,l anglers with the fly came and plied their craft. Many fine salmon have been caught there. An obi gentleman who lived near Market-gate wee egular visitor with his basket and fishing tackle. which it .. e a good jab for some poor I lad to carry,, for lie abeam I ..id them well. lientlemen would *me loom many places at a distance to have a few days' fishing at Warrington. Sperling!! also came up the Mersey to spawn. They came in large shoalA and were the most profitable fish to the poor fisherman. I have known some of them to earn £5O in a season by 'partings alone. After a very high tide we have taken many herring fry, and in the meadow., in Howley we have found a large quantity lathe drains when the tide was gon:.! clown. " " •• - -

Westy Reach, on the Mersey. This was so called from Westy Barn, an old barn which stood at the end. It belonged to M. Watt, of Fairfield, Warrington, who converted it no a cottage for an old fisherman and his trite to live in. Westy Reach was a great resort for graylings. Along its bank there wise long row of red willows, overreachingthe river, suarm- ing with small green grubs, which were constantly falling Mto the river when shaken by the mint. These were fine food for graylings. A particular kind rd fishing was re- quired for graylings, called "dibbing," anl was nice amuse.. went for the young ladies of Warrington of that ,lar, and there were always young gentlemen tm, to bait their hooks for them. You most have a nice pliant rod, code linerthout four feet long. If you look on the bark of the willow trees, you will find a little Wank tly, rather smaller than the com- mon house fly. It stands with its head down, which gives it the name of “down-looker.' Catch one, and put it on your hook then go silently to the edge of the bank, as near the trees as will allow your rod room to keep clear of the branches, and drop your tip to the surface of the water. With a trembling motion of the rod stand ready, for you witliornioly see shoals of graylings waiting. The moment your fly drops they watch it. little while, and (hen one of them makes a spring at your bait. With a drin hand, the fish is yours. This is “ clib-lishing," and fine sport it is.

But it 01105 mere neemsery to e.dinit, with every deal,. to make the best of the facts present,' to or, that ihs iin,nir.;„igi,. en is not yet even beginning to die. perse, whilst the unfavourable aspects of the Natimal Balance-sheet are still maititained. Sir Stafferd Northcom wee not particularly hopeful in his esti- mates loot March. Its fully allowed that the Revenue had for a time lost the remarkable einsticity which had been a special boast of English financiers, mil he even recognised the necemity of facing a fur- ther depreesion in the yield of the GAlea. But the Chancellor's estimates, timid as they were in some quarters supposed to be, turn out to have been much too sanguine. If we had a decrease of income last quarter, we have a still greater decream in the quarter ending on Weduesdoy last. Three menthe ago we bad occasion to comment on a falling off Which amounted to about £lOO,OOO. Now we are confronted by a net decrease, on comparing the returns of the past quarter with the correspoeding quarter of 1878, amounting to no lees than 4:453,000. This la the most etriking point in the Revenue Rs turns, but it is only as it were the fioiehing touch to a picture of gloom where"l the whole year has been busily supplying the detail.. A yet broader view of the figures issued from the Treasury on the closing day of loot year may be Vby contrasting the items due to direct and itt taxation with those which are due to the public services conilucted by the State. The revela- tion thus afforded is a most eignificaut and instruc- tive one. To petit in plain terms, every item of taxation chows a decrease, and every itern of service shows an Mermen. Wherever the Governineut has done work and been ;mid for it, it has earned a large amount of money. Wherever it has merely collected taxes from e distressed people, it has suffered a check and a disappointment. By the sale of Stamps for business transactions, succession duties, and the Ilk., we have made an allifillee of £117,000 on the past quarter, and of £349,050 on the post nine months, as compared with the same periods for the preceding year. By the working of the Post Office, we have increased our revenue on the nine months by £79,000, and ie the Telegraphic Service we have made an advance of £40,000. Turning now to the items of tmatiou, we fine that the Aeseesed Taxes lave yielded .411000 lem for the nine months; Customs have manifested a do. cross. of .E36ll,oeii, and Excise a decrease of no less then -P1,1371,000. Surely the leseon of these figures Is easy to read; iind it ought to strike our political financiers es sufficiently fray octant to justify snow departure in the whole eystan of national finance. Two things are especially cimr and beyond dispute. First, it is a fact that in every period of depression the revenue falls off to an alarming extent in the various items of taxation, nail above all in the items which depend up in the consumption of lux mies many of which, when consumed in muse. are posi- tively nosiom. Secondly, even in times of depres- sion the public mri ices conducted by the State are generally able to bold their owe, and men to show a steady increase, bemuse they depend on the more necessary operations of business, ou the transfer of property Mad 00 the Medea of intercommunication. We do not hesitate for a moment in saying that the truest wisdom would prompt auto make our revenue from public mrvices as mucl. as posaible rata.. our revenue from popular taxation. Na doubt it is well that imposts should be levied on certain articles of consumption, and particularly on those which are least necessary or beneficial to the consumers. But, confining ourselves for the present to the merely financial aspects of the question, it is demonstrated that the most trust- worthy and elastic sources of income are those which miring from service, and that the most fluctuating, as well ae the mast burdensome, are those which spring fnim taxation. If the adversity of the past few years proves any one thing more plainly than another it Is that the service of the public by the Suite is more satisfactory, as a commercial item in our accounts, thim any. other. It has been argued that the indefinite multiplication of these Stets (ser- vices would bran encroachment on the privileges of the public, nr of individuals, and that a Government cannot safely become a wholesale trader. We find no force whatever in such allegatione. The real public benefit of such sourcee of income as those which are furnished by the l'ost Office and Telegraphs is an un- mixed good, and vastly outweighs any hardship whiah may he inflicteol on individuale. Moreover, the scope for commercial enterprim in England is so unlimioal that the effect produced by a Government monopoly (for example) of the modes of inter-com- munication, from which an immeme revenue would be forth:wiling, would be absolutely insignificant. And if the Ihinemeuteon, by the wide mtension of its trading operations, could relieve us of some of the most objectiemble itnoosta now laid upon our shoul- ders, surely the nation at largo would be a gainer in every way. There is, of course, one item of direct taxation in which the past year shows a large increase of re- venue on the year which premiled it. This is the Item of lucome and l's party Tax, wherein the re- turns are swollen by the irnimiition of an additional twopence in the pound. Taking a comparison be- tween the whole year 1e79 and the whole year le7e, so as to include the fleet three months, in which the bulk of the tax la laid, we fled that the increase , amounts to .C3,454,000—that tit° say, over £1,725,000 for each penny of the rate. This may be regarded as satisfactory in proportion as the tax itself is satiefac- tory ; whereon we do not propose to expreee in this , place it very decided opinion. But even in respect ! of Income TAX. the receipts of the Government are considerable lees than they would have been if they I had not satered from the commercial drawbacks which have affected nearly every class of the in- habitants if this country. Look where we will, and taking our statistics from every available ssurce, we find that only a few individuals in a few favoimed trades have profited inatead of losing by the general depression, whilst in some eflalla the loesee have been enormous. To take an instance ; Mr. Seyd is accustomed to eupply us, at the end of each year, with some interesting figures relating to the commercial dimmers of the preceding terries months From the table. Just issued, it appears that 2,546 failures of wholeede firms hare been roc, rded in 1879, as compared with the stall higher figure of 3,013 in 1878. In the retail trades, hom ever, the number of fnilures was 14,101, as agaimt 12,410 in ISIS, and only 0,8.50 in 187 ii. The eignifi- canes of them figures will best once apparent, and it is not difficult to deduce the vest extent of the disaster implied in no much commercial disaster. Another indication of the same kind, bat doubtless affecting cimses which are not exclusively commer- cial, is afforded by she number of registered hills of sale—the proximate step to benkruptcy. Tnis num- ber has nmehed the almost unprecedented figure of 50,1010, which is an enormoue increase even on the number registered during the early part of 1,79. It is natural that with this actual or impending ruin so widely spread through the country, the takings of the let 'MA Tax collectors should have largely de- creased, at all events by comparison with what they would have been in °remain. times. We can only express a hope that, twelve months hence, it may be our pleasing duty to record a marked recovery from this gloomy condition of affairs, and that the finan- cial transactione of 1880 may be in every respect a thorough contrast with those of 1879. GREAT LIBERAL AIt:PING AT ST.
SPEECHES OF MAJOR EILKINGTON, MR BATH- BONE, M.P., M. W. S. CAINE, Mr. H. W. RILEY REV. 11. J. WEATHERUEAD, AND OTHERS.

Under the auspices of the St. Helena Liberal Association, large and enthusiastic meeting was held in the Town Hall on Thursday evening last. The ball was crowded, and the -oceedings were characteris.d by ardor and enthusiasm. The chair was occupied by Major Pilkington, and among a large number of gentlemen by whom he was supported on the platform were Mr. W. Rathbone, Ml'., Mr. W. S. Caine (Liberal candidate for Scarborough), Ilie Worsl,ipthe Mayor of Sr. Helens, Colonel Gamble (president of the Liberal Gab), the Rev. J. Brown, Rev. IL J. We:abed...oh Dr. kleNicol, Dr. Traylor.] ; Messrs. T. Cook, J. C. Gamble, R. Pilkingdon, A. Sinclair, G. Pore, Cook, Martin, Cotton, J. Boyden, Flint, Foote, It. J. Brook, P. Id. Wright, Hanson, P. Taylor, C. Sharpies, 11. R. Lacey, Allen, William (Amide, J. F. Hilton, B. A. Dtoingoole, neither, Jackson, W. H. Foster, 11'. Harlin., I'. Brown, Holm, P. McKinley, Dr. Jamieson, Dr. Gasket', Dr. Ricketts, de. In the body of the hall we noticed Be.. Donnell., Garton, the Revs. Father O'Reilly and Fa' her Baines, T. Wilshaw, ; Messrs. Polding, Newton, T. C. Wilcock, Riley, H. If. Barker (of the Examiner), it. Leach, ! J. H. Craikede. klajor PILIIINGTOW who was recdived with fond cheers, said he bode letter from Mn. Rylands saying that he was unable to attend, and he was extremely sorry to hear thin; also, one from Mr. Briggs, the member for Blackburn, to the same effat, and one from Mr. Meklinnies, of Warrington,' who, he was extremely sorry to say, was unable to be pre- sent. Ile had no doubt some people might wish to know what was the reason of holding 0 ineeting like that. It was quite evident that before the end of twelve months we must have a general election. Theie were signs all over the country. 01 11,, gteat contest, an,l Hoz lines of the campaign were peeno plainly laid down. (Cheers.) The Liberals were most ;determined to attack, and, he faned, to demolish pretty cons:derably the home and foreign policy of her Maj, sty's (jovernment. (Loud cheers.) The Tories, on the other hand, had determined to defend their foreign policy ; they look upon this as the great stronghold by which they hoped to return victorious at the end of the general election. No doubt there war, a great deal of chill in the selection of theid standard. The 'fortes would take a great deal of lodking after, yet he fancied that if Sir Stafford Northcote was asked his opinion of the state of the budget, be woold say, no doubt, " the leant said soonest mended." (Laughter and chews.) With regard to the foreign policy, he thought the Tories would dui leg the con. test try to draw the people's mind away frron the dangerous and insidious inmeri .1 policy at home. (Cheers nod hear,: hear.) We had already passed in our history through many a crisis. When old King John thought lie might have his own way', but his nobles made him sign the Mag. Charta— (cheers) ; when King Charles thought he might waste as mud, money as he liked, but the old Croniwellion Parlia- ment Bet him right about that question; and, corning lower down, James the Second, who endeavoured to carry out his departures in the government of the country, the Prince of Orangewas placed on the throne instead. It seemed to hinithe talk about the home aml foreign policy was absurdohnost absurd. The question WAS whether we shall have in office at home the initiators of this foreign policy ? Were our armies role moved about, treaties mode and ratified, and many things transacted indeed without the consent And nanction, and even without the very knowledge of the Parliament of this country. (Cheers.) He would say that if the present Goverhment did not acknowledge the rights and privileges of the English people he trusted that the English people would. (Cecers.) The 01,1 constitution was watched. eimugh with men like Sir Robert l'eel. Lord Pahnerston, anal the late Lir' of Derby; , and he did not think there mootany true born Englishmen who would hesitate lota moment Co cheese between the old constitution in this isle of ours MA the new (angled one headed IT one who had no mere English pride in las heart thrin British blood in his veins. (Loud cheers.) lhe Flirt . of Beaconsfield had boasted before this country as tieing the , friend of the English workingman. (Ilear.) Whether by his poll y Le Izad prolonged the del,ioalen in trade he did' • not know ; whethar he showed any particular enthusiasm for humanity undo great desire for the good of men generally • when lie turned a deaf ear to that report of the atrocities in , Bulgaria; when he goes into war with South Africa where thonsands of brave fellowe—as brave as any in England— (chrers.—were slaug,ldered; when !Lego. into a wanton and unjust war in Afghanistan where men and women mere starving in the cold anew. Whether this was any guarantee loony Englishman that lie coral for Hein lie .E.l not boo, • (Cheers.) But they Lancashire workingmen keesy better than that. (Cheers.) We had lad too famines ; them WAS a (amino in Ireland, in Europe, in Asi,t ; and we had tisthd the bitterness of distress in our own town and in the county. He woeld like then to know what WAS the stale of this canntry if it had not been for the cheap loaf if the Corn Laws had not been repelled. l'he amount of suf. feringand distrais that then existed no one could toll. Whose name did they put along with the reliever of that distress ? (A Voice z Cobden.) And they should not for- weenie name of the &at English gentleman—Sir Rolwrt Peel, who, against all his ',colons conviction!, agninst all Ids party ties, and risked them as he did, and his place and power, determine,d that the country should have the Corn Laws eel-staled. (Cheers.) They nhould remember also and see who so cruelly tainted him—( hear, hear)—end nzho fol- lowed him and hunted him out of place and power. It was Disraeli. (Cheers.) Contrast that conduct. With that of the Duke of Wellington,whoalthougha Conservative, came down tothe House with tears down his face, bore his testimony and the love and admiration he had for his friend Sir Rodot.Peel. Would the Duke of Wellington have landed ns in the help- less condition we were in in Afghanistan? Would he have taken the advice of Lords Lawrence and Northbrook, and with untried men have gene into one of the largest peas of the empire and attack All Shed? Would the Duke of Wel- ington with the view of ft ightening Europe have brought native troops to Malta ? Would the Duke of Wellington 113V9 gone to the Treaty of Berlin with a secret treaty in his pocket; and would he lave answered miestions ill the way Lord Iteaconsiiehl answere.l them in the House of Com- mons, and give a lie to the country ? (Cheers.) He thought not. Toryism had coot this country a good .leal, and in addition we had to give ep our national privileges and national honour ; and it was time that the Liberals went in and shoved the Teri. out. (Cheers.) He bad great Pleasure in calling upon their friend Mr. Rathbone, the Liberal member for Liverpool, to speak upon this subject. , (Applause.) Mr. W. RATWBOWI9, M.P., who wasreeeived with loud and prolonged cheering, said he o,oe pleased to have received Ruch a reception from the people of St. Helene, who were electors for south-went Lancashire. As they could net get a man ne big ot Mr. Gladstone to contest the division of south- west Lancashire, he WA9 glad to nee that they were deter- mined to return two men in his place. (Cheers and laughter.) He then moved the following resolutiou z—tt That this meeting protests against the dishonourable, disastrons, and extravagnnt foreign policy of the present Government, and deprecates itn indifference ta the principles of sound finance and to the claims of dsmestie legislation." He said—As an elector of south-wrst lanennhire, who has fought side by side with Mr. Sinclair in former battles,' have been entrustell with a resolution condemning alike the home and foreign] policy of the lievernment. When Mr. Sinelair asked me to meet you to-day, I responded most cordially, bemuse it is qnite time for the electors of south-west Lancashire to be stirring in preparation for the great .election which will settle some of the greatest harps winch have ever been placed before the country. In the Aurae of an experience now somewhat extended, lean only remember one or two occasione when every man elaitning to be a patriot had such a weight of responscbility thrown upon him. The issue which we have to determine I believe to be no less a one than this—is thineountry to retorn too period of peace and prosperity, or are we to continue under a foreign policy which keeps the country in 0 perpetual state of war atul insecurity, which renders prosperity impossible, and which has, so far, been unatten led with one single successful result ? When this meeting was arranged for, we had no idea thnt we should tonlay be in the midst of a contested eleaion for Liverpool, anii overt' important election it is going to he. Coming as it does just before the general eleotta, iesultmill he watched with deep interest everywhere hut nowhere, fleece,y more anxiously then in the goal Mum of St Helens z for whether you are going to fight as electors for the borough of St. Helens or for South- west Lancaaldre, I am sure you will take the warmest in- terests in th efforts of the Liberate of Liverpool to wrest its reprenentation froin Jingoism an.l Toryism. Let me tell yon. then, that are have got a fust.rate candidote, and we mean to win. Ile inn hearty. energetic Young sailor, who, though a lord and surroen,lai by all the 'temptations which wealth and pleasure offer to a man in his position. prefers hard work and bard fighting todawdling about and enjoying himself in the precincts of a court and so he has come to Liyerpoolothere he will liml plenty of hard work anti plenty of hard fighting. and I am sure we have your hearty go-d wishes for his success. As to the home policy of the Government, I shall not trouble you about that, as home policy they have none worth naming, except thatof keeping numbers of yon out of your votes, because they choose to call yen coanty voters, though you live inn large borough and have as good a right to yonr votes/es any other house- holder. borough or county. B 01! should like to say a few welds to you about their foreign policy, which, to my mind, is aismtashad as alternate timidity and rashness can make it. 11'e have had, recently. a very able and 0 very significant non-political speech from Lord Derby, full of that clear, practical common sense n hich we prise as one of thecharac- teristic qualities et our c, trot, z and I think we menet no better than Apply that speech. to the crisis now before us. It was entire...a with that great ratifier] for which Lord Derby is en remarkable; belt under that untion it is per- , teeny clear that it discloses n most sanguine vior of our possible future. 1 saw possible future, for, while nothing could be more encouraging than the brightness of the fleet part of his speech, he afterwards pointed out that the (unite prosperity of the country entirely depended upne our being allowed to use our industry, oar roterpriee, and our invention for our individual welfare and the common good, disturbed neither by netual wars nor by whalien, mischievons—a conatant sante of uneasiness and insecurity. It is well that no should remember, with Lord Derby, that at no period of our history have the English people been no poor, to miser- able. or so dissatisfied ns they were during the 15 or 20 years , which fellewed Warciloo. Therefore. when we have to con- sider the opportnnity chosen Ito the present Government for entering upon wars which Lord Derby dearly thinks a, wars not femora upon ns by duty or Pelf-defence. we must beer in mini that they have been undertaken et a period when this country is engaged in a life and death struggle with America and ite other Competitors for the maintenance of its indestrial norm icy. We all know that the money :Nen of war, and even the heavy taxation whh ic expenditure on war involves, are the leant part of its cost eec conntry like this. We are rich; and while moots, tier, net enterprise, and industry have fair play, we can Sod the money for war and bear the heavy tavtion which it in- volves. net if, ill the midst of an induatrial shrunk like thin, enterprise in paralysed by uncertainty. and attention in diverted from invention and improvement to the unhealthy exeitement of war, then sr, are pappina the very vitals of our nabonal strength szal eveatness. Yet these men, who peoless themeelves to Id Cens,,teative statesmen, choose this very lime of all ethers to manta and bring uppn us distur.

THE 0121ISEIHE RAILWAY CH.LISION.—Ihe collision on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway near Burscough Junction on Thursday evening turns out to have been much more diustrous than wee at tirst reported. In addition to the engine driver, guard, and stoker of the Liverpool train and the stoker of the express train, three passengers were killed, and the number of persons injured orrnn,ooio to seven.
