The London correspondent of Saturday's Liverpool Peg says!—l understand that a conference of the leaders of the Liberal party will take place in London about Mooday week. There will then Ito in town Mr. Gladstone, Lord Hartingtort, Mr. Bright, Mr. Forster, Mr. Lowe, and iii, W. Harcourt. The conference will have reference, of course, to the fortheoining nreeting of Parliament, and the attitude to be °torrent by the Opposition towards the Queen's Speech. The 3lessage from the Throne, will, it is expected, he of more than usual impor- tance no foreshadowing the probable intention of Ministers with regard to the dissolution, and also as afford- ' into, or not affordiog, some insight into the settlement of Attire in Afglmnistan. From all into learn in best informed quarters of the Liberal party, and, indeed. from personal conversation with influential metnhers of the Opposition, it seems likely that the foreign policy of the Government will be subjected to immediate attack by the Liberal chiefs in both Housesof Parliament; but no decision will be formally I arrived at until the conference.

lIMMESHIMATION OF LIVMIPOOt. : A COXING Svurnot.r. —The London correspondent of the Litarpoot Port of Saturday says :—The news of the death of Mr. Torr, and the creation thereby of • vacancy in the Parliamentary repro. sentaion of the great Mersey town, has created quite sen- sation in London. In Liverpool will now take place one of the roost exciting and important political contests in modern , eleMion annals. Rarely have I known anything to equal the feeling displayed Bile evening at the political clubs. On all hands the cry is that Liverpool will decide what Shot- field really meant—in other word., the Government, as far ,as one may judge from the excited uttermoes one hear, to- night, would almost formallv put on the Liverpool election the character etc public teat or trial of the feeling of the country. The opinion of long-beaded politicians lore is that in whatever way it ends, the Liverpool obeli. will pre- cipitate a dissolution. If the I.:overturn:Mare tielltert, they cannot stand amiinst the demands and tannin of the Liberal leaders. If they win, they are almost certain to take the event as an omen of luck, and go right ahead into a general ction. We are in for a fight which Min lie watched with the most intense anxiety by politicians of all classes in Great Britain.

Mr. Joseph Robinson, J. W. Wilson, Hugh Shaw, and others attended the meeting as a deputation from the owners of property in the district of Pecker's Hill and the North. East side of the of. Helens Junction Railway Station, who had been threatened with legal proceedings to restrain them from using the brook there as a sewer and for the convey., ance of drainage from their respective premises. Mr. Hone, the Surveyor' mid that all the drainage about Pecker's Hill ran into the Old Boook, and ultiwatcly dis- charges itself below Mpss Nook. Mr. ROBINSON stated that the deputation attended the meeting to :sk the Corporation to provide a sewer for the drainage of the district in question. The Mama said it was unfair that the Corporation should pay the cost of supplying a certain district which had not already got the means of getting their drainage essay. Mr. RILEY said he did not know whether he should be considered a jJant of the deputation or not—he being a repre- sentative for West Sutton—but he thought that if the authorities of the town in their wisdom thought proper to include Sutton in their borough limits it wis their duty to keep it too sanitary condition; and he thought that it was more in that reopect that It should he viewed than simply a question of expense. If anything injurious resulted from the nuisance it was Protrable that it would not be confined to Sutton but would affect the whole town. The MAYOR sahl they had Than° Heath, which was thickly populated, standing over, and yet the Council had done nothing yet on account of the large expense which it or ould entail, and the ratepayers would Im the first to grumble if they Clri out those improvements.
